title: Freddy Spaghetti

jokes.text: Ron tells Andy the building will hopefully be empty for months, clearly delighted by the government shutdown.
jokes.setup: Andy asks how long the shutdown will last, expecting a normal concerned response.
jokes.punchline: Ron, a libertarian who hates government, says 'if we're lucky, this building will be empty for months' with genuine enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Ron Swanson character comedy — his anti-government libertarianism means a shutdown is genuinely good news for him. The subversion of the expected 'this is bad' response is clean and well-executed, and the line could only come from this specific character.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: How long do you think the shutdown will last?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I hope it lasts for months. Shutting down the government is like my birthday and Christmas had a baby.

jokes.text: Andy brags about his 'super sweet-ass rad crotch rocket' motorcycle lease at 12% interest — 'one of the highest you can get' — as if that's a good thing.
jokes.setup: Andy excitedly announces he finally has a job and could afford his motorcycle.
jokes.punchline: He proudly describes getting 12% interest, identifying it as 'one of the highest you can get' with zero awareness that this is terrible.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Andy Dwyer character comedy — his cluelessness about basic financial literacy, expressed with pride, is deeply true to the character. Bragging about getting the worst possible interest rate as though it's an achievement is a genuinely funny inversion that only works for Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I got an amazing deal on this motorcycle! 24% interest rate!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Do you know how rare it is to get financing that good? That's basically the best rate out there!

jokes.text: 'Uh-oh! Nailed it.' — Andy apparently crashes his motorcycle almost immediately.
jokes.setup: Andy has just bragged about his cool motorcycle and riding ability ('it's just like driving half a car').
jokes.punchline: Cut to [00:50] where we hear Andy exclaim 'Uh-oh!' followed immediately by 'Nailed it.' — implying he crashed the bike right after leaving.
jokes.explanation: The extreme economy of this joke — two words of setup, two words of punchline — is brilliant. 'Nailed it' as Andy's damage-control response to an obvious crash is deeply character-specific and the structure (bragging followed instantly by failure) is textbook comedy. High rewatch value because you appreciate how tight the construction is.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Uh-oh.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Nailed it.

jokes.text: Leslie says no one is more upset about the parks closure than she is, then immediately qualifies: 'Not like it's a competition. Because if it was, I would win. But that's neither here nor there. The point is I would win.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining the seriousness of the park closure to the press/public.
jokes.punchline: She derails her own serious statement by insisting she would win a grief competition, then doubles down when she catches herself.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent Leslie Knope character comedy — her compulsive competitiveness overriding her self-awareness in real time. The escalation ('But that's neither here nor there. The point is I would win.') where she catches herself and then repeats the offense is perfectly constructed. Only Leslie Knope would turn a sincere expression of concern into a competitive boast. Quotable and deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Being upset isn't a competition.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But if it were, I would win. Twice.

jokes.text: Parent asks 'With the government shut down, who is going to stop Al-Qaeda?'
jokes.setup: A concerned citizen is asking what the parks closure means practically — where will her kids go during school break?
jokes.punchline: She suddenly escalates to global terrorism as a concern about the government shutdown.
jokes.explanation: A solid absurdist gag — the comedic logic of 'if the government is shut down, ALL government functions cease' is relatable, but the specific Al-Qaeda reference is a bit dated and the character isn't specific enough for it to truly land. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: So you're telling me the parks are closing? What's next, international terrorism?

jokes.text: Parent: 'Keep them in my house? Where I live?' as an apparent horror at the idea of spending time with her own children.
jokes.setup: Parent asks what she's supposed to do with her kids if the parks are closed all summer.
jokes.punchline: The clarification 'Where I live?' implies the very concept of being home with her children is so foreign and terrible it needs to be restated for emphasis.
jokes.explanation: The appalled clarification of her own address is a nice comedic beat — the economy of the joke is strong, and the implied horror is relatable. Not deeply original but well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.line: What am I supposed to do with my kids when the parks are closed?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Well, you could keep them in your own home.

dialogue.speaker: Parent
dialogue.line: The horror!

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I do not like having Freddy Spaghetti's blood on my hands.' Unnamed official: 'I believe you mean Freddy Spaghetti's sauce.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is dramatically lamenting the cancellation of the children's concert.
jokes.punchline: The official corrects her idiom for the pasta-themed children's entertainer — 'sauce' instead of 'blood.'
jokes.explanation: A clean, tight wordplay joke that earns its laugh through economy and perfect timing. The correction is unexpected enough to land well, and the absurdity of parsing idioms for a pasta-themed entertainer is charming. Not groundbreaking but a well-crafted quick joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have blood on my hands.

dialogue.speaker: Councilman Milton
dialogue.line: That's marinara sauce.

jokes.text: Cut to someone burning their tongue on food and saying 'Burned my tongue. Don't even care.'
jokes.setup: Presumably reacting to the 'Freddy Spaghetti's sauce' burn from the previous exchange.
jokes.punchline: The self-deprecating admission of injury paired with dismissive indifference, possibly a talking head treating a minor injury with dramatic resignation.
jokes.explanation: A mild reaction beat — the 'don't even care' dismissal of a self-inflicted minor injury is a competent but unremarkable joke. The context is unclear without more character identification, which weakens it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This coffee is way too hot, but I'm going to drink it anyway because I have a meeting in two minutes and I need the caffeine.

jokes.text: Chris complains about the color of a glass/mug: 'You see this color? I don't like it. It's too depressing.'
jokes.setup: Chris is about to receive a visitor in his office.
jokes.punchline: His complaint about the emotional impact of a water glass's color reveals his hyper-attentive, wellness-obsessed personality taken to an absurd degree.
jokes.explanation: A decent character-establishing moment for Chris — his obsessiveness over minute wellness details is in character, though this particular gag doesn't reach its full potential as a standalone moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Can I get some water?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, make it room temperature. No, slightly cool. But not cold. And it needs to be filtered. Well, purified. Actually, I need to know the pH level. It should be between 6.5 and 7.5. And please tell me where the water came from. I prefer water from a spring. A specific spring. In Switzerland. Actually, not Switzerland — that's too fancy. Maybe Vermont? No wait, the water needs to be alkaline. But not too alkaline. This is really important for my health and my body's optimal functioning.

jokes.text: Chris's elaborate, specific water order: cold, no ice, in a glass or mug with no handle.
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives for a meeting with Chris.
jokes.punchline: Chris interrupts the greeting to place a deeply specific, multistep water order — revealing his controlling, hyper-optimized personality.
jokes.explanation: The escalating specificity of the water order — cold, no ice (already contradictory/redundant), then the odd 'no handle' specification — is a nice character joke. The interruption of a professional greeting to micro-manage a water delivery is pure Chris Traeger.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you're not going to argue with me? You're just going to agree?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yeah, I think you're right.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I have a 40-slide PowerPoint presentation I've been working on all night, so I'm going to give it anyway.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I'm very glad that you agree with me, but I actually worked really hard on my argument. Is there any way I can still kind of...' Chris: 'Yeah?' Leslie: 'I'd love to hear it.'
jokes.setup: Chris immediately agrees with Leslie's request, before she can make her argument.
jokes.punchline: Leslie, who over-prepared, asks if she can still give her argument anyway — Chris agrees to listen, and she thanks him, revealing her performative diligence matters as much as the outcome.
jokes.explanation: A sharp Leslie character moment — her obsessive preparation means the argument itself is almost more important to her than the result. 'I'd love to hear it' delivered by Chris with genuine warmth makes the joke land perfectly. Deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Do you know what the problem with this town is?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's the government.

jokes.text: Chris talking head: 'The government has been shut for two days, and one city employee has tried to schedule 14 meetings with me. Can you guess who?'
jokes.setup: Chris mentions that one employee has been unusually aggressive about scheduling meetings.
jokes.punchline: The rhetorical 'Can you guess who?' — obviously Leslie — played with knowing amusement, is funny because the audience already knows exactly who it is.
jokes.explanation: A solid talking-head joke in the mockumentary tradition — the rhetorical question the audience already knows the answer to. 14 meetings in two days is a good specific number. Competent character comedy without being exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Guess who spent all night reorganizing her binders by color, thickness, and the emotional resonance of the topic?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That was me. I needed them organized that way.

jokes.text: Chris explains his daily 10-mile run: 'I have run 10 miles a day every day for 18 years. That's 65,000 miles. A third of the way to the moon. My goal is to run to the moon.'
jokes.setup: Chris mentions he has to go run his daily 10 miles.
jokes.punchline: He has done the math, traced the cumulative distance to a cosmic scale, and set an impossible extraterrestrial goal — all delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalation from '10 miles a day' to '65,000 miles' to 'a third of the way to the moon' to 'my goal is to run to the moon' is perfectly constructed. Each step is logical given Chris's obsessive self-optimization, but the endpoint — casually announcing a goal to run to the moon — is surreal and deeply funny. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific, and delivered with Chris's signature sincere intensity. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor example.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I've been training for a marathon, but I've decided to set an even more ambitious goal.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm going to run to the moon.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: It's 238,900 miles away, which means if I run 50 miles a day, I can make it there in about 4,778 days. That's only 13 years!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I've already started mapping out my route and I'm thinking of doing it completely chemical-free with a raw food diet.

jokes.text: Ben tells Leslie she's non-essential. Leslie protests. Ben: 'I know, it's on your badge.' Leslie looks at badge: 'This? This isn't me.'
jokes.setup: Ben tells Leslie she's not supposed to be in the building because she's non-essential.
jokes.punchline: He reveals it's printed on her badge. Leslie's denial — 'This? This isn't me' — is both a denial of the label and a slightly absurd claim about the badge itself.
jokes.explanation: A very clean joke — the reveal that 'non-essential' is literally on her badge is a good physical/visual comedy beat, and Leslie's indignant denial ('This isn't me') is perfectly Leslie. The economy of the exchange is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I've been thinking about the Ramsett Park project. We could really make a difference in this community.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we're not getting funding for that. We're not even on the radar.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But it's such a great idea. The people of Pawnee need this.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The people of Pawnee need a functioning sewer system. You're asking for a park. We're literally below the sewer on the priority list.

jokes.text: Chris arrives at Ann's hospital saying he 'ran by' and popped in — already at mile 9 — and he's not sweating at all. 'I have a resting heart rate of 28 beats per minute. The scientist who studied me said that my heart could pump jet fuel up into an airplane.'
jokes.setup: Chris casually mentions he ran by the hospital while doing his daily 10 miles.
jokes.punchline: Ann notes he's not sweating; Chris explains with absurd physiological claims, culminating in a scientist saying his heart could pump jet fuel into an airplane.
jokes.explanation: The jet fuel line is exceptional — it's specific, absurd, and perfectly delivered in Chris's style of self-impressed sincerity. The detail about 'the scientist who studied me' implies a whole separate absurd story. The joke escalates from mildly unusual (no sweat) to medically impossible (28 BPM) to completely surreal (jet fuel pump). Highly quotable and deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I am essential! I'm very essential!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, your badge literally says 'non-essential.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's just what they put on there. It doesn't mean anything.

jokes.text: Chris asks Ann on a date, citing the evidence that she was attracted to him when drunk: 'I think you might find me attractive because you got drunk and kissed me when we first met.'
jokes.setup: Chris wants to ask Ann out.
jokes.punchline: He marshals the evidence with the logical rigor of a scientist — specifically her drunk kissing him — as a neutral data point, completely missing the social awkwardness of the observation.
jokes.explanation: A solid Chris character joke — his clueless sincerity in presenting 'you kissed me while drunk' as logical evidence of attraction is funny. Not among the episode's best but competently executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This isn't even my badge. I've never seen this before in my life.

jokes.text: April to Ann, after Chris leaves: 'That's the guy who likes you, that you're not into.' Ann: 'Yeah.' April: 'And which part of him are you not looking at?'
jokes.setup: Ann insists she's not interested in Chris.
jokes.punchline: April, with her signature dry wit, notes that Ann is clearly checking Chris out — the specific 'which part of him' phrasing is both pointed and funny.
jokes.explanation: April's deadpan delivery makes this land well. The joke is sharp and economical — 'which part of him' implies Ann is staring and highlights the hypocrisy. Very April Ludgate in its dry, slightly mean specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: My resting heart rate is 48 beats per minute. That's lower than most Olympic athletes.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's impressive, Chris.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Thank you. In fact, I'm so efficient that I've been pumping my own blood into the jets at the airport. Saves the city thousands on fuel.

jokes.text: Ann explains she makes 'reckless' decisions at the end of relationships. Then: 'So I need to stay away from Chris.'
jokes.setup: Ann is explaining why she's vulnerable after a breakup.
jokes.punchline: The 'reckless thing' turns out to be pursuing a stunningly attractive, enthusiastic man — framed as a dangerous impulse to resist.
jokes.explanation: A competent setup-punchline joke playing on Ann's relatable post-breakup recklessness, but the punchline (Chris is the 'reckless' choice) is a bit obvious. Functional situational comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ann, I have calculated that you are 94% compatible with me based on my analysis of your physical attributes, career trajectory, and potential for bearing healthy offspring. I would like to take you to dinner. No pressure though.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris, that's... that's a lot of pressure.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm confused. I explicitly said no pressure. My tone was very casual.

jokes.text: Mark reveals he quit the city and took a buyout to work for Norton Construction — but first, there's an awkward pause as the camera catches Leslie processing this.
jokes.setup: Mark is in the middle of the chaos at Ann's backyard; Leslie asks what he's doing.
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Mark has quit, while Leslie has been fighting to keep the department alive, lands as a tonal shift punctuated by the silent reaction beat.
jokes.explanation: More of a dramatic beat than a joke, but there's comedy in the contrast between Leslie's all-in effort and Mark's quiet exit. The awkward pause carries the humor. Not a strong joke on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I avoid Chris because he's reckless. He does these crazy things like eat a salad for lunch and go to bed at a reasonable hour.

jokes.text: Leslie says 'I guess I've been mispronouncing your name all these years. Mark Brendana-quitz.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is processing Mark's departure and says goodbye.
jokes.punchline: She deliberately mispronounces his famously unpronounceable last name as 'Brendana-quitz' — a joke about names that are hard to say, and perhaps a gentle affectionate tease.
jokes.explanation: A mild wordplay moment — the 'quitz' ending makes it sound like he's quitting, which has a double meaning. Cute but not especially sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I'm working for a private contractor now.

jokes.text: Mark talking head: 'Ann broke up with me the week I was going to propose, the government got shut down, and yesterday one of those pigeons took a [shit] on me. And I was indoors.'
jokes.setup: Mark explains he was looking for a sign to leave his job.
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of catastrophes culminates in being defecated on by a pigeon — indoors — as the final straw and cosmic sign.
jokes.explanation: The 'and I was indoors' button is the key to this joke's success — it transforms a standard litany of bad luck into something genuinely surprising. The impossibility of being hit by a pigeon indoors is the perfect absurdist escalation. Well-structured with a strong button. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Mark, I just realized I've been saying your name wrong this whole time. It's actually pronounced 'Quits,' isn't it? Because you're quitting!

jokes.text: Leslie deduces Tom is about to have sex because 'Boyz II Men's On Bended Knee' is playing.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to figure out if Tom is busy.
jokes.punchline: Leslie identifies the Boyz II Men slow jam as the specific indicator of incoming sex — delivered as matter-of-fact deductive reasoning.
jokes.explanation: A solid joke — the Boyz II Men reference is both character-specific for Tom and a funny observational point. Leslie's flat deduction makes it land as character comedy for both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I got bird poop on me. Indoor bird poop. That's impossible.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Which somehow makes it worse.

jokes.text: Leslie advises Tom: 'Don't make it last really long. Ladies don't like that.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says she just wants to give Tom 'a little advice.'
jokes.punchline: The advice — that women don't like sex to last a long time — is delivered with Leslie's earnest authority, subverting conventional wisdom with cheerful obliviousness.
jokes.explanation: A funny subversion — Leslie's confident, authoritative tone on a subject she clearly has unconventional views about is amusing. The joke depends on character voice more than originality.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, you're about to have sex.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? No, I'm not.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're playing Marvin Gaye. Nobody plays Marvin Gaye unless they're about to have sex. It's a scientific fact.

jokes.text: Talking head about Leslie: 'Leslie's usually already up and often she's already on her way over.'
jokes.setup: Character explains that Leslie is the kind of friend you can call in the middle of the night.
jokes.punchline: The qualifier that she's 'already on her way over' implies Leslie proactively shows up before being summoned — a funny escalation of her hyper-eager personality.
jokes.explanation: A solid character joke about Leslie's intensity. The escalation from 'already up' to 'already on her way over' is a nice structure, implying Leslie anticipates her friends' crises.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, I'm just going to say it. When you're with a man, you need to take charge. Be aggressive. Grab him by the—well, you know. And don't be shy about telling him what you want. Men respond to confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Also, never let him see you eating. Men don't like that. Just consume nutrients intravenously before dates.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And wear something that shows you're fun, but not too fun. You want to seem like you might do something crazy, but you won't actually do it. It's a delicate balance.

jokes.text: Leslie describes the ideal man as 'six feet tall with wild, crazy hair and a ukulele that doubles as a water gun' — revealing she's talking about Freddy Spaghetti.
jokes.setup: Leslie says the only guy she cares about right now is a tall man with crazy hair.
jokes.punchline: The description sounds like a romantic interest until 'ukulele that doubles as a water gun' reveals it's a children's entertainer.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed misdirection — the romantic-sounding description pivots cleanly to reveal Freddy Spaghetti. The specificity of 'ukulele that doubles as a water gun' is the perfect absurd button. Pure Leslie Knope in how seriously she takes a children's entertainer.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm always there for my friends at night.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm so intense I'm already coming over.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'You know what is [a priority]? Sewage. Pawnee's kids are less important than poop tubes.'
jokes.setup: Children's concerts aren't a priority in the budget crisis.
jokes.punchline: Leslie sarcastically summarizes the government's priorities as choosing sewage ('poop tubes') over children — the juxtaposition of bureaucratic infrastructure with the blunt term 'poop tubes' is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Poop tubes' as the official name for sewage infrastructure is a great comedic choice — the contrast between bureaucratic language and this blunt, childlike term is funny. Sarcasm delivered with conviction.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: She's describing Freddy Spaghetti, the children's entertainer

jokes.text: 'Pawnee's kids are less important than poop tubes.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is describing what takes priority over children's concerts
jokes.punchline: 'Pawnee's kids are less important than poop tubes.'
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economical line. 'Poop tubes' is a great choice of words — technical enough to be slightly absurd, crude enough to be funny. The moral indignation framing makes the word 'poop' land even harder.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Look, I know it sounds terrible, but we have to prioritize the sewage system over the children's programs. It's just math.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Poop has to go somewhere. Children are optional.

jokes.text: Leslie calls Ann a 'devious bastard' for suggesting the lot behind her house as a concert venue.
jokes.setup: Ann makes a perfectly reasonable and simple suggestion.
jokes.punchline: Leslie treats it like a stroke of criminal genius, calling Ann a 'devious bastard' — the grandiosity of the compliment vs. the simplicity of the idea is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A nice quick joke — Leslie's hyperbolic response to a simple idea ('devious bastard') is perfectly Leslie, treating every solution like a heist. Quotable in the right circles.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, that's... that's the most brilliant idea anyone has ever had in the history of ideas. Your house? Of course! Why didn't I think of that? You're a genius. A beautiful, smart genius. I'm going to throw you a parade. Actually, two parades. One after the other. We'll shut down the entire city.

jokes.text: Leslie's A/B/C/D breakdown: 'A, yes. B, even if they don't, we'll just put the concert on ourselves. But C, yes. Yes, they're definitely going to show up. Although, D, maybe not.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks if anyone will show up to help.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's rapid-fire lettered list immediately contradicts itself — from confident yes to 'although, D, maybe not' — revealing her anxious optimism.
jokes.explanation: A delightful structural joke — Leslie's numbered lists are a character trait, but here the list undercuts her own confidence in real time. 'Although, D, maybe not' is the perfect self-defeating button. Deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, first of all, I think waffles are a perfectly acceptable dinner. Second of all, and I cannot stress this enough, waffles should never be eaten for dinner.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Third, government spending is out of control and needs to be cut. Fourth, we need to immediately increase funding for all local parks and recreation departments.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Fifth, I am completely objective and unbiased. Sixth, anyone who disagrees with me is wrong and probably a bad person.

jokes.text: Leslie says 'God bless you, Jerry Gergich!' and Tom's reaction: 'Wow. I never thought I'd hear those words from you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is worried no one will show up; Jerry arrives first.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's genuine gratitude to Jerry — normally the butt of jokes — surprises even Tom, who articulates the audience's reaction.
jokes.explanation: A nice running gag payoff — Jerry is perpetually underappreciated, so his arrival being met with genuine gratitude (and Tom's meta-commentary) is a warm, funny moment. Works best for fans of the show.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, did I just say something nice about Jerry? Oh my God, I need to sit down.

jokes.text: April arrives and says 'I still might not [help].'
jokes.setup: Leslie expresses surprise and pleasure that April showed up.
jokes.punchline: April immediately hedges — she hasn't committed to helping, just to showing up.
jokes.explanation: Three words that are perfectly April — her refusal to commit to enthusiasm is a tight character joke. Maximum economy, high character specificity, though not a complex joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, I'm so glad you're here to help with this!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not here to help. I'm just here.

jokes.text: Leslie asks Jerry how he feels about lifting heavy things. Jerry starts: 'My doctor just said I should avoid...' Leslie: 'Being a wuss? Yes, I agree.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Jerry to do physical labor; Jerry starts to cite a medical restriction.
jokes.punchline: Leslie cuts him off with a fake completion of his sentence — 'Being a wuss?' — then pretends that was the medical advice.
jokes.explanation: A solid running-gag structure — Jerry's mistreatment is a show staple, and Leslie cutting off his medical excuse with 'Being a wuss?' is a clean, well-timed gag that fits both characters perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My doctor says I should—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, your doctor also thinks you're a human being worth listening to, so clearly his medical degree is from a very stupid hospital.

jokes.text: Ron talking head: 'I am an official member of a task force dedicated to slashing the city budget. Just saying that gave me a semi.'
jokes.setup: Ron describes his role on the budget-cutting task force.
jokes.punchline: 'Just saying that gave me a semi' — Ron's anti-government libertarianism manifests as genuine physical arousal at the prospect of cutting the budget.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a genuine Parks and Rec classic. The joke is perfectly economical — Ron's joy at government reduction is so complete that it becomes sexual. The delivery (deadpan, matter-of-fact) is crucial. This is pure Ron Swanson character comedy at its highest level: the libertarian ethos taken to its logical, absurd extreme. 'Just saying that gave me a semi' could only come from this character. High quotability, deep character integration, clean structure. Justifiably near the episode's top score.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: He's literally sexually aroused by cutting government

jokes.text: Ron's budget idea: 'Right off the bat, we sell City Hall. Let somebody turn it into a large gas station or a T.J. Maxx.'
jokes.setup: Ron is asked for budget-cutting ideas in the task force meeting.
jokes.punchline: His first idea is to sell City Hall and let it become a T.J. Maxx — the specificity of T.J. Maxx (a discount retailer) makes it funnier than any generic store would be.
jokes.explanation: The T.J. Maxx specificity is what elevates this — Ron could have said 'a store' or 'a mall' but T.J. Maxx captures the perfect tone of Ron's practical indifference to government prestige. It's not a luxury store, not a joke store — it's just a normal, slightly down-market retail choice that says everything about Ron's view of government. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We should sell some government property. I suggest we start with the old quarry, that pit of raw sewage behind the rec center, and whatever that smell is coming from the Parks Department bathroom.

jokes.text: Ron's phone ring tone interrupts the budget meeting. He answers immediately with 'Don't cut anything without me.'
jokes.setup: The budget task force is having a serious meeting.
jokes.punchline: Ron's ringtone interrupts, and his first priority upon answering an unrelated call is to issue a warning not to cut the budget without him — revealing that government reduction is his primary concern above all else.
jokes.explanation: A solid character moment — Ron's instant 'don't cut anything without me' reveals his priorities humorously. Works as a character joke but doesn't add much new to what we know about Ron by this point in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And here we are, folks, at the construction site. I'm about to hammer this nail. It's a big moment. The nail doesn't know it yet, but its life is about to change forever. I'm picking up the hammer now. Feel the weight of it in my hand. The responsibility. I'm raising it up... up... the nail is waiting, wondering what will happen next. And now... I'm bringing it down with the force of a thousand suns!

jokes.text: Andy's bounce house needs '16 minutes for premium bounce.'
jokes.setup: Setting up for the concert, Andy is inflating a bounce house.
jokes.punchline: '16 minutes for premium bounce' — the specificity of '16 minutes' and the phrase 'premium bounce' as a genuine technical standard is funny.
jokes.explanation: A small background joke — the phrase 'premium bounce' as a technical standard is mildly funny. Doesn't land as a major joke but adds to the absurdist texture of the concert setup.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Freddy Spaghetti? That's a real person?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I just got my car detailed. I can't have some guy named Freddy Spaghetti eating marinara in my Lexus.

jokes.text: April asks if someone can pick up Freddy Spaghetti in their Mercedes and notes he is 'notoriously funky.'
jokes.setup: The team is figuring out logistics for getting Freddy Spaghetti to the concert.
jokes.punchline: 'Notoriously funky' — the idea that a children's entertainer has a known, documented smell problem is absurd and funny.
jokes.explanation: 'Notoriously funky' implies a reputation that precedes him and that the Parks team has specific prior knowledge of this children's entertainer's hygiene issues. The absurdity of this context is delightful.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So I took my girlfriend to this amazing restaurant last night. Best dinner ever.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And then this morning we had breakfast in bed together. If you know what I mean.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And by that I mean we literally had breakfast in bed. Eggs, toast, the whole thing. It was very intimate.

jokes.text: Tom about his girlfriend Lucy: 'We had dinner last night and breakfast this morning. What were we doing in between? Sex stuff.'
jokes.setup: Tom introduces Lucy to the group, who are surprised they had dinner together.
jokes.punchline: Tom's faux-rhetorical question followed by 'sex stuff' — delivered as a casual announcement to coworkers — is funny in its transparency.
jokes.explanation: 'Sex stuff' as the casual professional disclosure is classic Tom oversharing. The faux-rhetorical structure (asking a question he immediately answers) works well. Not highly original but well-executed.

jokes.text: Lucy's talking head: 'You guys know Tom really well, so I don't have to apologize for his behavior, right?'
jokes.setup: Tom has just announced to his colleagues that they had sex.
jokes.punchline: Lucy addresses the camera directly, relieved she doesn't have to apologize for Tom because everyone already knows he's like this.
jokes.explanation: A nice quick talking-head joke — Lucy's resigned acceptance that Tom's behavior requires no apology because everyone knows him is a meta-comment on the character. Works well as a one-liner.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I just realized we have a logistical problem. We're expecting 300 people at the harvest festival and we only have one bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? Where are they going to go?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I was thinking your house is pretty close by...

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: No! Absolutely not. 300 strangers are not using my personal bathroom.

jokes.text: Leslie announces 300 people will need to use Ann's house as the bathroom. Ann: 'Wait, aren't we expecting like 300 people?' Leslie: 'Hopefully! Okay, back to work!'
jokes.setup: Leslie announces the porta-potty situation; Ann realizes the implication.
jokes.punchline: Leslie cheerfully confirms 300 people will use Ann's house as a toilet, then immediately pivots to 'back to work!' before Ann can object.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's breezy 'Hopefully!' and rapid topic change before Ann can process the horror of 300 strangers in her bathroom is a great moment. The 'back to work!' is a perfect Leslie deflection. Character-specific and structurally clean.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Riding a motorcycle is like... it's like a woman, you know? You gotta treat it with respect, keep your hands steady, and if you don't wear protection, you're gonna have a bad time. Also, sometimes it leaks fluid and you have to take it to a guy named Pedro.

jokes.text: Andy explains riding a motorcycle: 'It's just like driving half a car.'
jokes.setup: Someone asks if Andy knows how to ride a motorcycle.
jokes.punchline: 'Half a car' — Andy's simple-minded but not-entirely-wrong characterization of a motorcycle as a fractional automobile.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical — five words that capture Andy's entire character. It's both dumb and weirdly logical, which is the Andy Dwyer sweet spot. The joke is also foreshadowing his inevitable crash.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Why didn't you return my calls?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I didn't want to talk to you.

jokes.text: Andy tells April he called her 'a gajillion times.' April: 'I'm so sorry. I was too busy not wanting to talk to you.'
jokes.setup: Andy confronts April about ignoring his calls.
jokes.punchline: April's deadpan apology-that-isn't: she was 'too busy not wanting to talk to you' — a perfectly April non-apology that names her deliberate avoidance as the obstacle.
jokes.explanation: 'I was too busy not wanting to talk to you' is an exceptional line — the structure of apologizing for being busy while naming deliberate avoidance as the activity is logically perfect and deeply April. It's technically an apology that is also an insult. Highly quotable, perfectly economical, completely character-specific. One of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ann, you deserve a good guy. Someone who treats you right, respects you, and makes you happy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? I know a guy. He's really into you. He's got a good job, he's stable, he's—well, he's me. I'm suggesting we have sex.

jokes.text: Tom to Ann: 'A girl like you can have whatever guy she wants.' Then immediately: 'Because I could definitely talk to Lucy about a three-way situation.'
jokes.setup: Tom gives Ann a genuinely sweet pep talk about her worth.
jokes.punchline: The sweet moment immediately collapses when Tom suggests a threesome with Ann and his current girlfriend — revealing his sincerity was always a prelude to a proposition.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from genuinely warm to immediately inappropriate is a great Tom Haverford moment — it suggests the sweet speech was always going somewhere. The 'I'm kidding. But serious at the same time.' button makes it even better. Good escalation structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Okay, I have a great idea for team building. We're all going to pair up and do a trust fall, but here's the twist—we're going to do it blindfolded, and the person catching you will be behind you, so you have no idea where they are or if they'll actually catch you. Then, we're going to go back to my place and do some trust exercises in a hot tub.

jokes.text: Ben suggests loosening up their brains with a 'massage train' — and announces 'Ron Swanson is the locomotive.'
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to get the budget meeting unstuck.
jokes.punchline: The suggestion of a massage train is absurd enough; casting Ron — the most stoic, anti-touch character — as the locomotive is the perfect specific absurdity.
jokes.explanation: The visual of Ron Swanson leading a massage train is delightful — the casting is everything here. Ron, who would hate this activity most, being designated the engine is a great character-specific absurdist choice.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We could sell the animals to a circus.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ron, no.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A testing facility?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ron!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A restaurant?

jokes.text: Ron suggests selling zoo animals to 'cosmetics labs? Weird restaurants?'
jokes.setup: The task force is looking for budget options other than firing Leslie.
jokes.punchline: Ron's alternative budget ideas include selling zoo animals to animal testing labs and 'weird restaurants' — the specificity of 'weird restaurants' is the dark button.
jokes.explanation: 'Weird restaurants' as an option for exotic animal acquisition is a great dark comedy beat — it's specific enough to conjure a real image (exotic meat restaurants) while being sufficiently oblique to be funny rather than offensive. Pure Ron in its casual disregard for sentimentality.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm using reverse psychology on you.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm telling you the opposite of what I want so you'll do what I actually want.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's... that's just psychology.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, it's reverse psychology.

jokes.text: April confesses her feelings to Andy using 'reverse psychiatry' as her approach strategy.
jokes.setup: The Andy/April romantic tension has been building.
jokes.punchline: April calls her strategy 'reverse psychiatry' — a malaproprism for 'reverse psychology' — and the term is both wrong and somehow right for April's affect.
jokes.explanation: 'Reverse psychiatry' is a nice malapropism that works for April — she's pretending to be disaffected when she actually cares. The word choice feels intentional and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy has unresolved feelings about Ann. He's not over her. Until he figures that out, he's just going to keep dating people who remind him of her in some way. And that's not fair to whoever he's with.

jokes.text: Long awkward pause after April says yes she likes Andy, then Andy slowly asks her to go out
jokes.setup: April and Andy have just admitted they like each other
jokes.punchline: Extended pause before Andy's painfully slow, formal invitation: 'So, then perhaps, shall we go out this evening?'
jokes.explanation: The comedic payoff here is Andy's uncharacteristically formal phrasing ('perhaps, shall we go out this evening') after an extended silence. The awkward pause is a good structural beat, and Andy's formal register is funny coming from him specifically.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: These budget cuts are a righteous war against government waste.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And I intend to fight it with every ounce of my being.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Or, at the very least, I would if I wasn't so lazy.

jokes.text: April immediately says 'No' to going out with Andy after agreeing she likes him
jokes.setup: Andy, emboldened by April's 'yes,' asks if they should go out that evening
jokes.punchline: 'No.' — April's flat refusal directly after admitting she likes him
jokes.explanation: The immediate reversal from 'Yes I like you' to 'No' we shouldn't go out is perfectly April. The joke is in the speed of contradiction and the logic she then provides (she thinks he still has feelings for Ann). The one-word punchline after the dramatic pause-and-yes sequence is exceptional structural comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, actually, Leslie is unique. There's only one Leslie Knope.

jokes.text: Ron talking head: 'Because of my libertarian beliefs, Leslie does 95% of the work. So you should lay me off. I'd be proud to be a casualty in this righteous war.'
jokes.setup: The task force is discussing who to lay off to save Leslie's job.
jokes.punchline: Ron volunteers to be fired on the grounds that his own ideology requires he do minimal work — framing his layoff as a principled sacrifice.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Ron Swanson character comedy — he volunteers for layoff as a principled stance, citing his libertarian beliefs as justification. 'I'd be proud to be a casualty in this righteous war' frames budget cuts as a noble cause. The logic is perfectly circular and deeply character-specific. Only Ron Swanson would argue for his own firing on ideological grounds.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: They're coming!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, are the Russians here? Did Gorbachev finally make his move? I knew it. I KNEW IT. We should have invested in more bunkers. Why didn't anyone listen to me?

jokes.text: Ben: 'Every department is losing a Leslie Knope.' Ron: 'No, Ben, they are not. No other department has one to begin with.'
jokes.setup: Ben argues that all departments will suffer equally from cuts.
jokes.punchline: Ron's flat correction — that Leslie is irreplaceable not just within her department but unique across all departments — is delivered as a simple factual correction, not a compliment.
jokes.explanation: This is a beautiful Ron Swanson line — coming from a man who normally dismisses everything about government, his quiet insistence that Leslie is uniquely irreplaceable is both funny (for its deadpan delivery and logical structure) and genuinely moving. The joke works on two levels: it's Ron being logically precise AND Ron revealing he values Leslie more than he lets on. Exceptional economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I get death threats all the time. It's just part of the job.

jokes.text: April accidentally tells the state auditors about the illegal concert while 'trying to save some government jobs' — delivered with her characteristic flat affect.
jokes.setup: The state auditors suddenly arrive at the concert setup.
jokes.punchline: April reveals she accidentally (or carelessly) tipped off the auditors, then adds 'It's been a very strange day for me' — as if the main inconvenience is to herself.
jokes.explanation: 'It's been a very strange day for me' as the button to causing a crisis is perfectly April — the self-centered framing of a problem she caused is funny. The detail that she did it 'in an attempt to save some government jobs' makes the incompetence more specific.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The main performer just cancelled. He's sick.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's fine. I can do it. I'm very talented.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, you can't even carry a tune.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well... how hard could it be?

jokes.text: Chris addresses the crowd with enthusiastic support: 'You are all super amazing... totally supportive of your inspiring efforts!' Then immediately hands off to Ben: 'Now, my partner Ben wants to say something.' Ben: 'Yeah, we're shutting this down.'
jokes.setup: Chris hypes up the crowd with over-the-top positivity.
jokes.punchline: The immediate pivot to Ben announcing the shutdown contradicts every word Chris just said. The juxtaposition of Chris's boundless positivity with Ben's flat cancellation is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The Chris/Ben dynamic is perfectly encapsulated here — Chris's manic positivity immediately undercut by Ben's deadpan shutdown announcement. The structure is excellent: build up the crowd, then immediately crush them. 'Damn!' from the crowd is the perfect reaction. High impact from the comedic contrast between the two characters.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is the most beautiful venue I've ever seen. The acoustics, the lighting, the way the books are arranged by the Dewey Decimal System... it's perfect. I'm going to cry. Actually, I'm already crying.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's a library.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A LIBRARY, Tom. A library.

jokes.text: Ben explains the Chris and Ben partnership: 'When he would do it by himself, nothing got done, and when I did it by myself, I'd get death threats. Together, it seems to work.'
jokes.setup: Ben explains how he and Chris work as a budget-cutting team.
jokes.punchline: Ben casually mentions receiving death threats when working alone — delivered as a neutral workplace observation — before concluding the partnership 'seems to work.'
jokes.explanation: The death threats being mentioned as a casual efficiency problem rather than an existential concern is perfect deadpan. 'Together, it seems to work' as the understatement button is excellent. The joke reveals the stakes of budget-cutting in local government through understatement.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to change the inappropriate lyrics in this song.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, what do you want to change?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How about we replace 'sexy' with 'esty'?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: 'Esty'? That's not a word.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's better than sexy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Is it though? 'You're my esty lady'? That doesn't help at all.

jokes.text: Freddy Spaghetti canceled the concert to take a gig in Eagleton — at a library. Leslie: 'That's literally the worst place I can imagine.'
jokes.setup: The team learns Freddy Spaghetti took another gig.
jokes.punchline: The rival city Eagleton is already a running source of contempt; Leslie's addition that a library is 'literally the worst place I can imagine' (worse, presumably, than anywhere) is a hyper-specific Pawnee-centric burn.
jokes.explanation: The Eagleton rivalry is a running gag throughout the series; adding 'at a library' as the specific insult is a nice layering of contempts. Works best for fans who know the Eagleton dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what they say in show business: 'It's not about the destination, it's about the friends you make along the way.'

jokes.text: Andy: 'I don't even have children's songs. My last song I wrote was called Sex Hair.' Leslie: 'Well, just take the word sex and change it to pickle.' Andy: 'Pickle?' [sings] 'You got pickle hair, baby / And you got it from me.' 'Yeah. Still sounds like it's about sex.'
jokes.setup: Andy is reluctant to play a children's concert because he doesn't have appropriate songs.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'just change sex to pickle' solution is immediately tested by Andy — and the substitution makes the song no less suggestive, which Andy correctly notes.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent comedy bit. Leslie's naive solution, Andy's immediate field test of the substitution, and his accurate observation that it still sounds sexual is a perfect three-beat structure. 'Pickle hair' is an inherently funny phrase, and the song sounding equally innuendo-laden despite the swap is a great comedic payoff. Both characters are perfectly in character. One of the episode's standout moments.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Freddy couldn't make it tonight. He's in the hospital with a severe case of linguine syndrome.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The doctors say if we don't get him on a strict penne-cillin regimen immediately, he could develop full-blown fettuccine fever.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's touch and go, but we're staying optimistic. The prognosis is... al dente.

jokes.text: Andy breaks both bones in his right arm and four in his hand falling off his motorcycle — just before he's supposed to play the concert.
jokes.setup: Andy agrees to play the concert and rushes off to get his guitar.
jokes.punchline: He returns (or is reported to Ann's hospital) with a catastrophic number of broken bones from the motorcycle he was bragging about — the callback to the earlier crash jokes.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of injuries (six bones broken) is funny in its specificity, and this is a callback payoff to the motorcycle jokes that opened the episode. The timing — right when Andy's guitar skills are urgently needed — is good structural comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's a firm handshake. My father always said a firm handshake is the mark of an honest man.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Of course, he also believed that the government was using handshakes to inject tracking devices into our wrists, so...

jokes.text: 'That's the side that hurts.' — Andy's response to being told he has broken bones in his right arm and hand.
jokes.setup: The doctor lists Andy's injuries (two broken bones in his arm, four in his hand).
jokes.punchline: 'That's the side that hurts' — Andy confirms the injury with cheerful, useless obviousness.
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — five words that perfectly capture Andy's simple-minded obliviousness. The observation is true but useless, delivered with Andy's characteristic guileless sincerity. A small but excellently crafted character joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you're talking about. That's just a turkey leg with bacon on it.

jokes.text: Leslie asks if Andy can be fixed in the next 10 minutes. Doctor: 'Sure, I'll just advance medical science 30 years.'
jokes.setup: Leslie desperately asks how soon Andy can be healed and play the concert.
jokes.punchline: The doctor's sarcastic response — 'Sure, I'll just advance medical science 30 years' — is a perfect deadpan burn on Leslie's wishful thinking.
jokes.explanation: A clean sarcasm joke with good economy. '30 years' as the specific advancement required is a nice detail. The doctor's deadpan is perfectly matched to Leslie's absurd optimism.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This week has been crazy. It's like I was a horse, and someone just shot me in the head.

jokes.text: Mouse Rat tried to play without Andy once. They called themselves 'Rat Mouse' — 'and they're awful.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Mouse Rat can play without Andy.
jokes.punchline: The band's emergency alternate name — 'Rat Mouse' — is just the words reversed, implying their creativity is as limited as their ability. The flat 'and they're awful' button is perfect.
jokes.explanation: 'Rat Mouse' — the words simply reversed — is a great throwaway joke about the creative limitations of Andy's bandmates. The specificity that they actually tried this and it was terrible adds to the absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: A-Cakes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh my god, you remember that?

jokes.text: 'There's an old saying in show business. The show must go wrong. Everything always goes wrong, and you just have to deal with it.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to reassure the team in the face of setbacks.
jokes.punchline: She misquotes 'The show must go on' as 'The show must go wrong' — then doubles down on the misquote as wisdom, explaining that everything always goes wrong.
jokes.explanation: The misquote that accidentally becomes a more accurate description of the situation is a nice joke — 'the show must go wrong' as an inadvertent truth about this particular concert. Leslie's confidence in delivering a mangled idiom is perfect character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Mean Ben? That's what you call me?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, yeah. When you're being all serious and bureaucratic.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I have spent years trying to earn your respect, and this is what I get? Mean Ben?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not a bad thing! It's like... it's sexy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It is not sexy. It's mean.

jokes.text: The backup performer introduces herself as 'Renata Ricotta.'
jokes.setup: Freddy Spaghetti has canceled; an alternative performer arrives.
jokes.punchline: The replacement is another Italian-food-themed children's entertainer — 'Renata Ricotta' — as if this is a whole genre of performer.
jokes.explanation: The existence of a parallel Italian-food-themed children's entertainer as the backup is a delightful absurdist detail. It implies an entire ecosystem of food-named children's performers that the Parks department casually taps into.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: As a government official, I believe in providing services to the public.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But Leslie, your singing voice is not one of those services.

jokes.text: Renata Ricotta explains that Freddy Spaghetti 'bumped his noodle' and that 'there was sauce everywhere. It was just streaming out of his face. It was really scary.'
jokes.setup: Renata covers for Freddy Spaghetti's absence.
jokes.punchline: The description of 'sauce streaming out of his face' — applied to what is clearly a head wound or illness — uses the pasta metaphor to describe something that sounds horrifying. 'It was really scary' is the earnest button.
jokes.explanation: The extended pasta metaphor for what sounds like a traumatic medical incident ('bumped his noodle,' 'sauce streaming out of his face') is a nice dark comedy bit. The commitment to the bit — including 'it was really scary' — sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, I need to tell you something. I kissed Ann.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: When?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A while ago. Before we were together.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So you're telling me this now... why?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Because I want to be honest with you. I love you and I don't want secrets between us.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, I'm pregnant.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: ...I also kissed her that one time last week.

jokes.text: Freddy Spaghetti arrives despite having 'bumped his noodle' — revealing someone paid him a 'much better offer.' Freddy: 'I am all about the money, babe.'
jokes.setup: The team was told Freddy Spaghetti took another gig and couldn't come.
jokes.punchline: Freddy appears, revealing he was bought out of his other gig — and breaks character by announcing 'I am all about the money, babe' — a cynical disclosure from a children's entertainer.
jokes.explanation: The cynical children's entertainer who is purely mercenary is a funny character subversion. 'I am all about the money, babe' from a pasta-themed kid's performer is a nice tonal contrast. The callback resolution works well.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Don't. I don't want to hear it. I know what you're going to say, and I don't want to hear it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I wasn't going to say anything.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Exactly. That's the worst part.

jokes.text: Ron's handshake introduction to Lucy: 'My father told me that a limp handshake was for weak men and Communists. He hated both.'
jokes.setup: Tom introduces Lucy to Ron; Lucy gives an 'impressive handshake.'
jokes.punchline: Ron's compliment escalates from a handshake compliment to a cold war ideology statement — delivered as though it's a normal paternal wisdom to pass down.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Ron Swanson lines — 'He hated both' is a perfectly economical button on a joke that reveals Ron's family background as an ideological firearm. The matter-of-fact delivery of anti-Communist handshake philosophy as normal paternal advice is both funny and completely Ron. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So what did you think of the Elton John concert?

dialogue.speaker: Child
dialogue.line: It was great! My favorite song was 'Tiny Dancer.' But I kept thinking it should be called 'Tiny Dancer... with Linguine!'

jokes.text: Ron Corleone introduction: Tom presents Ron to Lucy as 'Ron Corleone'
jokes.setup: Tom introduces Ron to his girlfriend Lucy
jokes.punchline: 'Ron Corleone' — Tom gives Ron a Godfather-themed nickname, which actually fits Ron's stoic, powerful persona
jokes.explanation: Nice quick joke. 'Ron Corleone' works because it's both Tom's typical nicknaming behavior AND because the Godfather comparison is unexpectedly apt for Ron's demeanor.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: You know what? I liked it better as a pit.

jokes.text: Tom reveals the turkey leg with bacon is called 'a Swanson' — Ron silently approves.
jokes.setup: Ron notices that Tom's turkey leg appears to have bacon on it.
jokes.punchline: 'They call it a Swanson' — a food item named after Ron Swanson, as if his meat preferences are so well-known they've become a menu item.
jokes.explanation: The idea that Ron's carnivorous preferences are famous enough to name a food item after him is a lovely piece of world-building comedy. 'Wow.' as Ron's reaction (presumably awed/pleased) is the perfect silent button. Deeply character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Mark, I got you a going-away present. It's a roll of red tape.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Red tape?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's a metaphor for bureaucracy. You know, all the red tape you have to cut through in government.

jokes.text: Ann brings Andy 'every color of Jell-O' — 'The Jell-O rainbow' — as a hospital gift.
jokes.setup: Ann visits Andy in the hospital.
jokes.punchline: The gift is specifically all colors of Jell-O — 'the Jell-O rainbow' — which is both a hospital-appropriate gift and oddly touching in its specificity.
jokes.explanation: A sweet visual gag — the 'Jell-O rainbow' is a specific enough image to be funny, and the hospital context makes it appropriate. More warm than hilarious, but it lands.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, why are you dressed like you just had sex at a country club?

jokes.text: Andy: 'You know when you're just already having a bad day and then you break all the bones in your arm because you crash your motorcycle?' Ann: 'Dude, that's what my whole week has been like. My life is a motorcycle crash right now.'
jokes.setup: Andy is commiserating with Ann about his injury.
jokes.punchline: Ann relates to 'break all the bones in your arm' as a metaphor — using 'motorcycle crash' as an emotional metaphor — while Andy meant it literally. The two are speaking at cross purposes about different levels of catastrophe.
jokes.explanation: A nice cross-purpose comedy moment — Andy's literal injury becomes a metaphor for Ann's emotional state, with the two characters connecting across very different registers of suffering. Not the sharpest joke but emotionally resonant.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I need to sit down.

dialogue.speaker: Character
dialogue.line: Ron, what's wrong?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's my ex-wife. Tammy Two.

jokes.text: Ann almost calls Andy 'A-Cakes' — she catches herself; he prompts her; she says it; they share a tender-but-awkward moment
jokes.setup: Ann and Andy have a charged moment that reminds them of when they dated
jokes.punchline: Ann almost uses his old nickname 'A-Cakes,' stops herself, gets prompted, says it — the nickname is both affectionate and revealing
jokes.explanation: Warm cringe comedy. The nickname 'A-Cakes' is funny in itself; the awkward dance around saying it adds cringe-discomfort value. More emotional than purely comedic, but the nickname lands a genuine laugh.

jokes.text: Ann's horrified reaction after the accidental kiss — apologizing repeatedly ('Oh my God. I'm... I'm so sorry. I should not... I'm sorry. That was not...')
jokes.setup: Ann and Andy have just accidentally kissed.
jokes.punchline: Ann's repeated failed attempts to complete an apology — never finishing a sentence — captures the comedic horror of the situation. The escalating incomplete sentences are the joke.
jokes.explanation: A cringe-comedy moment that works more as character acting than as a written joke. The inability to complete a sentence is relatable and funny but not exceptionally crafted.

jokes.text: Ben and Chris arrive at the concert and exchange pasta types: 'Spaghetti.' 'Fusilli.' 'Egg noodles. Egg noodles.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Chris arrive as the children are enjoying the concert.
jokes.punchline: Rather than normal greeting/commentary, they exchange pasta names as if participating in the ambient pasta-themed atmosphere — Ben saying 'egg noodles' twice with additional earnestness.
jokes.explanation: A mild absurdist bit — the two adults exchanging pasta names in greeting/appreciation is a low-key funny moment. 'Egg noodles. Egg noodles.' repeated with conviction is the best part.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Mean Ben has a soft spot.' Ben: 'Is that what you guys call me?' Leslie/Others: 'No. No, no, no. Mean Ben?'
jokes.setup: Ben has secretly paid to bring Freddy Spaghetti to the concert.
jokes.punchline: Leslie accidentally reveals the team calls him 'Mean Ben' while trying to compliment him — then everyone unconvincingly denies it.
jokes.explanation: A nicely executed moment — the accidental slip followed by the overcorrection denial ('No. No, no, no. Mean Ben?') is a classic Parks and Rec bit. Ben's wounded 'Is that what you guys call me?' is the perfect straight-man reaction.

jokes.text: Chris to Freddy Spaghetti: 'The biggest service was getting you to stop singing.'
jokes.setup: Ben says to Leslie that 'a service' was provided. Someone notes the pasta names being called out.
jokes.punchline: Chris, normally effusively positive, flatly delivers the backhanded compliment that the best service was the concert ending.
jokes.explanation: A competent deadpan joke from Chris — his normally relentless positivity briefly gives way to genuine criticism. The character contrast is the source of the humor.

jokes.text: Andy and April sneak off to Ann's house: 'Hey. Wanna go to Ann's house?' 'Seriously? Yeah. Move! Excuse me.'
jokes.setup: The concert is winding down; Andy and April have unresolved romantic tension.
jokes.punchline: The completely casual, unromantic way Andy propositions going to Ann's house — and April's 'Seriously? Yeah' — followed by them barging through the crowd, is funny in its anti-romantic directness.
jokes.explanation: A nice character moment — the total absence of romance in Andy's 'Wanna go to Ann's house?' is perfectly Andy, and April's immediate 'Seriously? Yeah' is perfectly April. The crowd-shoving exit is a good physical comedy cap.

jokes.text: Andy confesses to April that he kissed Ann 'like two minutes ago' — April: 'What?' Andy: 'She kissed me.' April: 'Okay, bye.' Andy: 'Wait, where are you going?' April: 'Bye.' 'No, no, no...' 'Bye!'
jokes.setup: Andy wants to be honest with April because he likes her so much.
jokes.punchline: He reveals the Ann kiss immediately, derailing the romantic moment. April's escalating 'Bye' as she leaves while Andy chases her is a perfect comedic escalation of disaster.
jokes.explanation: The perfect disaster structure — Andy sets up the romantic moment ('I want to be totally honest because I like you so much'), then immediately detonates it. April's repeated 'Bye' while Andy desperately protests is escalating comedy gold. The callback to the accidental kiss pays off immediately and catastrophically. One of the episode's funniest sequences.

jokes.text: Chris shows up at Ann's door — Ann: 'Dude, don't even think about kissing me.'
jokes.setup: Ann has just accidentally kissed Andy and is reeling from the chaos.
jokes.punchline: Chris arrives and Ann immediately pre-empts any romantic move — a callback to all the kiss/relationship chaos of the episode.
jokes.explanation: A nice callback button — Ann's immediate defensive 'Dude, don't even think about kissing me' after all the kiss chaos is a good quick gag. The timing makes it land as a funny button on the episode's Ann storyline.

jokes.text: Tom shows up at Ann's house, introduces his girlfriend Lucy. 'Tom Haverford. Who's your friend?' Tom: 'What the hell? Get out of here, dude!'
jokes.setup: Tom arrives at Ann's with Lucy; Chris is already there.
jokes.punchline: Chris greets Tom and immediately asks to be introduced to Lucy — apparently undeterred by Tom's protest. Tom's 'Get out of here, dude!' is answered with Chris's cheerful compliance.
jokes.explanation: A competent joke about Chris's social obliviousness — he cheerfully moves on after being told to get out. The gag works but doesn't add much beyond the character beat.

jokes.text: A child's favorite song from the concert: 'Penne and the Jets.'
jokes.setup: A child is asked what her favorite song was.
jokes.punchline: 'Penne and the Jets' — a parody of Elton John's 'Bennie and the Jets' with pasta substituted — is a great quick gag from a child character.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words that land a complete joke. The Elton John parody is well-chosen (the song title's 'B' sound swaps cleanly to 'P' for Penne), and having a child casually name-drop it is a great setup. One of the best quick jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Suck it, Paris, France.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is thanking the crowd and declaring Pawnee the greatest city in the world.
jokes.punchline: 'Suck it, Paris, France' — directed at no one present, addressed to a city on another continent, as if Paris, France is Pawnee's real competition.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly economical character joke — 'Suck it, Paris, France' captures Leslie's grandiose local patriotism in five words. The specificity of 'France' (as opposed to just Paris) is the perfect absurd detail. This is deeply Leslie Knope and effortlessly quotable. One of the episode's most memorable lines.

jokes.text: Mark: 'I liked this a lot better when it was a pit. Is that weird?'
jokes.setup: Mark and Leslie are having a bittersweet farewell at the lot that Leslie turned into a concert venue.
jokes.punchline: Mark, who watched the lot as a pit for a season, admits he preferred the pit — undercutting Leslie's achievement with casual, earnest anti-enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: A nice season callback — the pit has been a running element, and Mark's preference for it is both funny and a little poignant for a character who preferred the status quo. Works best for regular viewers.

jokes.text: Leslie gives Mark red tape as a going-away gift: 'So you'll never forget your roots.'
jokes.setup: Mark and Leslie exchange farewell gifts.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's thoughtful going-away gift is literally red tape — bureaucratic red tape as a sentimental keepsake for a departing government employee.
jokes.explanation: A lovely conceptual joke — gifting literal red tape as a government keepsake is original and very Leslie. The sincerity of 'so you'll never forget your roots' delivered without irony makes it funnier. The dual meaning of 'red tape' (obstacle vs. physical object) is cleanly exploited.

jokes.text: Leslie arrives at the budget meeting as Ron's 'official Parks and Rec representative.' Ben: 'That's only supposed to be... Essential personnel?' Leslie: 'Yeah. Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Leslie was declared non-essential and barred from the building.
jokes.punchline: Ron has found a workaround — by making Leslie his representative, she's now technically essential. The callback to the 'non-essential' badge joke lands with extra satisfaction.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback payoff — Ron's bureaucratic workaround to get Leslie back in the building is both in-character (Ron values Leslie despite himself) and a clean structural callback to the non-essential badge joke. Leslie's self-satisfied 'Yeah. Yeah.' is a great button.

jokes.text: Ben notices an autographed picture of Jamie Foxx: 'Is this an autographed picture of Jamie Foxx?' Chris: 'There it is. Thank God.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Chris are settling in for their budget work.
jokes.punchline: Chris has apparently been waiting for someone to notice his autographed Jamie Foxx photo — 'There it is. Thank God.' implies he was desperate for the acknowledgment.
jokes.explanation: 'There it is. Thank God.' implies Chris has been anxiously waiting for the photo to be noticed — the relief in his response is the joke. A small but effective character beat revealing Chris's need for attention/validation.

jokes.text: 'So how long is this shutdown going to last? No idea. I might have to get a temp job. Maybe I should start working on my cologne line.'
jokes.setup: The shutdown continues with no end in sight
jokes.punchline: Tom's contingency plan is his cologne line — a typical Tom Haverford side-hustle that sounds exactly like something he'd actually pursue
jokes.explanation: Solid Tom Haverford character beat. His cologne line as a backup plan is perfectly calibrated to his entrepreneurial delusions. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Tom talking head: 'Whenever Ron has sex, the next morning, he comes in dressed like Tiger Woods.'
jokes.setup: Tom introduces an observation about Ron's behavior.
jokes.punchline: The specific tell — dressing like Tiger Woods (golf attire) as Ron's post-coital uniform — is absurd in its specificity and implies a long-established pattern.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The Tiger Woods post-sex tell is highly original — the specificity of golf attire as Ron's intimate victory uniform is both unexpected and completely believable for the character. Tom's casual, matter-of-fact delivery of this absurd insider knowledge is perfect. The joke implies a whole history of this happening and everyone knowing about it. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: 'Oh, God. What? Who is that? That is my ex-wife.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just walked in triumphantly dressed as Tiger Woods (implying sex)
jokes.punchline: His ex-wife appears — immediately threatening his good mood
jokes.explanation: Strong episode-ending topper. The immediate reversal of Ron's good fortune — ex-wife arriving right after his Tiger Woods victory lap — is a classic sitcom cliffhanger beat. The escalating reactions ('Oh, God. What? Who is that?') before the reveal are well-structured. Works well as both joke and season finale hook.

jokes.text: Ron enters, Ben asks 'You all set?' and Ron looks horrified — revealing his ex-wife is in the room.
jokes.setup: Ron enters dressed like Tiger Woods looking pleased; Ben greets him normally.
jokes.punchline: Ron's mood instantly shifts when he apparently sees his ex-wife — 'What? Who is that?' 'That is my ex-wife.' — the Tiger Woods celebration immediately deflated.
jokes.explanation: A great season finale button — Ron's post-sex triumph immediately encountering his ex-wife is a classic comedic deflation. The episode ends on a cliffhanger that's also a joke. The Tiger Woods outfit becoming even funnier in retrospect (he celebrated prematurely) adds rewatch value.

tmdb_overview: When Ben prevents Leslie from holding a children's concert, she takes matters into her own hands. Mark makes some big decisions about his life, and Andy gets some unexpected romantic attention.
insight: Absurdist character comedy anchors a 68-joke finale that underperforms on impact despite solid density.
